terms.comment: Rome knew rising prices, above all of grain: cāritās annōnae, the opposite of vīlitās, cheapness. It names the high prices, not the steady fall in the value of money. Its other sense is love, affection.
Egger’s phrase, built on classical vīlitās (Cic.), for the cheapening of money itself.
A calque on the modern word; classically īnflātiō is a swelling up, and flatulence (habet īnflātiōnem magnam is cibus, of beans, Cic. Div. 1.62).

phrases.latin: cum alter annus in vīlitāte, alter in summā cāritāte fuerit
phrases.english: when one year saw low prices and the next the very highest

phrases.latin: tanta repente vīlitās annōnae ex cāritāte reī frūmentāriae cōnsecūta est
phrases.english: so great a fall in the price of food followed at once on the dearness of grain
phrases.source: Cic. Imp. Pomp. 44 (Lewis & Short, s.v. vīlitās)
